Q: Does lock blocking make a ModifiedDate watermark sync safe? A:

When a new row is inserted into the table, the row gets an X lock.

The reason you are seeing this behaviour is that you don't have an index on ModifiedDate, so the SELECT needs to scan the whole table, at which point it gets blocked by the X lock. When the lock is released it continues.

You should have an index anyway, to make this more efficient.

CREATE TABLE dbo.MyTable
(
    Id            int IDENTITY(1,1) NOT NULL,
    Name          varchar(50)       NOT NULL,   
    ModifiedDate  datetime NOT NULL DEFAULT (GETDATE()),
    CONSTRAINT    PK_MyTable PRIMARY KEY CLUSTERED (Id),
    INDEX IX_ModifiedDate (ModifiedDate)
);

Now you should find that a SELECT which seeks after your new value will not be blocked.

The real solution to your problem is that the SELECT is wrong. The client should hold on to the most recent row it receives, and seek from that and order the rows in ModifiedDate order. At which point it will get blocked again by the new insert. So it never misses an earlier row which was committed later, as such a row will have always blocked the previous SELECT from proceeding until it is committed.

SELECT * 
FROM MyTable
WHERE ModifiedDate > '2026-07-26 04:00:00'
ORDER BY ModifiedDate;

What you do need to be careful of is creating the ModifiedDate not at the same time as the insert. For example:

DECLARE @modified datetime2 = SYSUTCDATETIME();

-- do long running stuff

INSERT MyTable ...

In this case, whether or not you use a transaction, you may still miss the row, as it's not been locked in any way.

Q: I have a working docker-compose.yaml - what specifically will kompose convert NOT carry over into production-grade Kubernetes manifests? A:

Short version: treat kompose convert output as a draft starting point, never a finished prod manifest. Here's the concrete list of what doesn't survive the trip, and why.

1. depends_on is ignored. Kubernetes has no direct "start B after A" primitive, so ordering simply isn't emitted. You handle startup order differently — init containers, or (better) app-level retries. For a service that talks to Postgres, that means reconnect-with-backoff until the DB is up, not a depends_on.

2. build: does not build an image. Kubernetes can't build from source. The image must be built and pushed to a registry the cluster can reach before you apply anything. Locally that's a built-in registry (e.g. k3d-registry.localhost:5000).

3. network_mode: host and custom networks map poorly onto the Kubernetes networking model or are dropped.

4. Bind mounts aren't preserved. Instead of mounting local files, you're expected to use a ConfigMap or Secret.

5. The big one — the output has no production spine. Generated manifests come by default with no requests/limits, no liveness/readiness probes, and environment variables in plaintext instead of a Secret. Those are exactly the things that make a manifest behave like prod.

So a reasonable workflow:

# generate a DRAFT only, then harden it by hand
kompose convert -f compose.yaml

Then, on the generated files, you add: resource requests/limits, liveness + readiness probes, move credentials into a Secret, replace bind mounts with ConfigMap/Secret, add an Ingress, and decide startup ordering via init containers or retries.

A related pin worth knowing while you're setting up a local cluster to test all this: when you pin the Kubernetes version, Docker tags can't contain +, so it's rancher/k3s:v1.31.5-k3s1, not v1.30.2+k3s1.

I wrote a full breakdown of what "production-like" should and shouldn't reproduce, with this Kompose gap list and a checklist, here: https://dorokhovich.com/blog/local-k8s-production-like-environments?utm_source=stackoverflow&utm_medium=community&utm_campaign=local-k8s-production-like-environments

Q: Skip parameter based on cell value? A:

Using the regular SUMPRODUCT function (or plain old SUM if using Excel 2021 or later) enables you to bypass the IF functions, and have multiple sets of optional criteria:

The formula in J7 is

=SUMPRODUCT(E2:E10*SIGN((NOT(J2))+(A2:A10=I2))*SIGN((NOT(J3))+(B2:B10=I3))*SIGN((NOT(J4))+(D2:D10=I4))*SIGN((NOT(J5))+(C2:C10=I5)))

and illustrates the impact of individually activating each of 4 optional criteria.

Q: Change a variable based on two conditions A:

You can use case_when() from {dplyr} as it's the cleanest way to handle multiple conditional value pairs.

library(dplyr)
catdat <- catdat %>%
  mutate(variable_name = case_when(
   # put all conditions ex.
   female == 0 & lab_hb < 13.5 ~ 0, # male, 
   anemia)
  )
